title: Bengaluru Techie Lands O-1 'Einstein' Visa After Three H-1B Lottery Rejections
excerpt: IBM engineer Tanush Sharanarthi, 26, secured the extraordinary ability visa after three consecutive years of H-1B lottery failures, highlighting a growing alternative pathway for skilled Indian professionals.
body:
• IBM engineer Tanush Sharanarthi, 26, from Bengaluru secured an O-1 "extraordinary ability" visa after being rejected three consecutive years in the H-1B lottery.
  • Sharanarthi built his O-1 case over six years through AI research publications, hackathon judging, journal peer reviews, and open-source contributions.
  • The O-1 visa has no annual cap and costs roughly $12,000 in total fees — a fraction of the now-contested $100,000 H-1B fee imposed by the Trump administration.
  • Immigration experts say the O-1 pathway is gaining traction among Indian STEM professionals frustrated by the H-1B lottery's randomness.

A 26-year-old Bengaluru-born software engineer working at IBM in California has secured the coveted O-1 visa — often called the "Einstein visa" — after three straight years of failing to win the H-1B lottery, offering a blueprint for skilled Indian professionals seeking alternatives to the increasingly uncertain H-1B route.

Tanush Sharanarthi shared his journey on LinkedIn, where his post quickly went viral among the Indian tech community in the United States.

"For three years straight, I played the H-1B game of chance. Three tickets, three misses. At this point, I was starting to feel like the unluckiest person in Vegas."

— Tanush Sharanarthi, IBM engineer

From Lottery Frustration to Extraordinary Ability

Sharanarthi, who holds a master's degree from Johns Hopkins University, told Business Insider that the H-1B lottery felt like "playing the slots in Las Vegas — you win sometimes, but mostly you lose and have no control." The H-1B program offers just 85,000 visas annually through a randomized lottery that regularly draws hundreds of thousands of applicants.

Rather than waiting on luck, Sharanarthi focused on building credentials that would qualify him for the O-1 visa, a category reserved for individuals with "extraordinary ability" in sciences, arts, education, business, or athletics. Unlike the H-1B, the O-1 has no annual cap and no lottery.

"Instead of waiting on luck, I went all in on what I could control: late nights, building products, publishing research, and contributing to the field I love," he wrote. "Turns out, consistency pays better than the lottery."

Six Years of Groundwork

The O-1 visa requires applicants to demonstrate extraordinary ability by meeting at least three of eight eligibility criteria. Sharanarthi explained that much of the work he had been doing naturally aligned with the requirements.

"I had published work on artificial intelligence, I used to judge hackathons, and I used to review papers for other conference journals. I had about six years of contributions to my field in AI under my belt," he told Business Insider.

His portfolio spanned his time at Kimberly-Clark, his graduate studies at Johns Hopkins, and his current role at IBM. He applied for the O-1 visa in August and received approval in less than two weeks, according to NewsPoint.

"I wasn't doing work solely for a visa," Sharanarthi said. "My focus has always been on my field, AI and software engineering. Along the way, I've worked on research papers, contributed to open-source projects, reviewed papers, and judged hackathons. These were things I was already doing, but they lined up well with the O-1 requirements."

A Cost-Effective Alternative

The O-1 visa also presents a significant cost advantage. While the Trump administration's September 2025 proclamation imposed a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visas — a fee that a federal appeals court has since blocked as an unlawful tax — the O-1's total processing costs average around $12,000, including legal fees and the $250 integrity fee, according to immigration experts.

That cost differential, combined with the lottery-free process, has made the O-1 increasingly attractive to qualified professionals. The Daily Jagran reported that Sharanarthi's story inspired widespread congratulations on social media, with many professionals asking him for tips on the visa process.

What This Means for Indian Tech Workers

Sharanarthi's experience highlights a growing trend among Indian STEM professionals who are turning to alternative visa categories as the H-1B program faces mounting uncertainty. The FY2027 H-1B cap was recently reached with no second lottery, while a proposed Senate bill seeks a three-year pause on new H-1B visas entirely.

For those considering the O-1 route, Sharanarthi offered practical advice: "The main thing would be to focus on your domain and working on projects that can help tick off multiple criteria. For example, working on a good project can help you write a paper and share with the community while at the same time showcase that your work is original."

He emphasized that the O-1 is built on merit, not luck. "My advice is not to do it just for the visa. Be passionate about your field and contribute to it. The rest follows."
nri_angle: The story resonates with thousands of Indian tech professionals in the US stuck in the H-1B lottery, offering the O-1 visa as a viable alternative pathway built on merit rather than luck.
author: Diaspora Desk
